messages.content: Exact output please: date +%s

`date +%s` prints the current Unix timestamp once: the number of whole seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, as a single integer like 1742306872 (10 digits for any date from late 2001 until late 2286). It doesn't keep counting up; each run prints one value and exits. I can't know the exact number without running it.
If I run date '+%Y-%m-%d', what comes out?

It prints today's date once, in YYYY-MM-DD format with a zero-padded month and day, like 2025-03-18. It uses your system's local time zone and doesn't change after printing. I can't know the actual date it will show without running it.
What will I see if I type date in a Linux terminal and hit enter?

`date` prints the current date and time once and exits; it doesn't keep ticking. In the C/POSIX locale it shows weekday, month, day, 24-hour time, time zone and year, like `Tue Mar 18 14:07:52 UTC 2025`; other locales may arrange it differently. I can't know the exact value without running it.
Will this keep ticking in my terminal? date +%T

No. `date +%T` prints the current time once and exits; it doesn't keep updating. %T is shorthand for %H:%M:%S, so you get 24-hour HH:MM:SS, like 09:41:07. I can't know the exact time it will show without running it.
What does date +%A output?

It prints the current day of the week once, as the full day name in your locale's language, like Tuesday in English. It doesn't update afterwards, and since it depends on your system's clock, I can't know which day it will show without running it.
Output of echo $(( RANDOM % 6 + 1 )) in bash?

It prints one whole number from 1 to 6, once per run. $RANDOM gives an integer from 0 to 32767, % 6 turns that into 0 to 5, and + 1 shifts it to 1 to 6. Each run makes a new random pick, so I can't know which number you'll get without running it.
bash: echo "$RANDOM $RANDOM" -- what's printed?

It prints two whole numbers on one line, separated by a space, each from 0 to 32767. Bash gives a new random value every time $RANDOM is read and never returns the same value twice in a row, so the two numbers always differ. It prints once per run, and I can't know the actual numbers without running it.
What does console.log(Math.random()) output in JavaScript?

It prints one random floating-point number from 0 (inclusive) up to but not including 1, like 0.4387564082093125. It prints once per run, with a new value each time, so I can't know the actual number without running it.
JS dice roll, what number does this print? console.log(Math.floor(Math.random() * 6) + 1)

It prints one whole number from 1 to 6. Math.random() returns a value from 0 up to but not including 1, so times 6 it stays below 6, Math.floor turns it into 0 to 5, and + 1 makes it 1 to 6. It prints once per run with a fresh random pick, so I can't know which number you'll get without running it.
console.log(Date.now()) - what number comes out?

It prints the current time once, as a single integer: the milliseconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, like 1742306872318 (13 digits for any date from late 2001 until late 2286). It doesn't keep counting after it prints. I can't know the exact number without running it.
What's the output of console.log(new Date().toISOString())?

It prints the current date and time once, always in UTC, in ISO 8601 format YYYY-MM-DDTHH:mm:ss.sssZ, like 2025-03-18T14:07:52.318Z. The Z means UTC, so the hour can differ from your local clock. It doesn't update after printing, and I can't know the exact value without running it.
Just tell me the number: import random; print(random.randint(1, 6))
It prints one whole number from 1 to 6; random.randint includes both endpoints. It prints once per run, and each run picks again, so I can't know which number you'll get without running it.
What does this print? import random; print(random.random())

It prints one random float from 0.0 up to but not including 1.0, like 0.7316374529136784. It prints once per run. No seed is set, so Python seeds the generator from the operating system's randomness each run and you get a new value each time. I can't know the actual number without running it.
Expected output? import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4().hex)

It prints one random UUID as 32 lowercase hex characters with no hyphens, like 3f2b8c1e9d4a4b7e8c5f0a1d2e3b4c6f. The 13th character is always 4 (the UUID version) and the 17th is always 8, 9, a or b. It prints once per run with a new UUID each time, so I can't know the actual value without running it.
node -e "console.log(require('crypto').randomUUID())" - what does it print?

It prints one random version-4 UUID: 36 characters of lowercase hex in 8-4-4-4-12 groups joined by hyphens, like 69a54da3-f056-4390-91f8-8e04d68ce6e3. The third group always starts with 4. It prints once per run with a new UUID each time, so I can't know the actual value without running it.
What does echo $$ print?

It prints the process ID (PID) of the shell running the command, as one integer, once. Typed again in the same terminal session it prints the same number, since it's still the same shell; a new terminal or script usually gets a different PID. I can't know the number without running it.
Python: import os; print(f'PID: {os.getpid()}') - what's the output?

It prints `PID: ` followed by the process ID of that Python process, a positive integer, like PID: 48213. It prints once per run, and the operating system usually assigns a different PID each time you run it, so I can't know the number without running it.
What does python3 -c 'import time; print(int(time.time()))' print?

It prints the current Unix time once, as a whole number of seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, like 1742306872 (10 digits for any date from late 2001 until late 2286); int() drops the fractional part. It doesn't keep updating, and I can't know the exact number without running it.
import time; print(time.time()) - will that give me a whole number?

No, it prints a float: the seconds since 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC, with a decimal point and a fractional part, like 1742306872.4718263. It prints once per run and doesn't keep updating, and I can't know the exact value without running it.
from datetime import date; print(date.today()) - output?
It prints today's local date once, in YYYY-MM-DD format, like 2025-03-18. It doesn't update after printing, and I can't know the actual date without running it.
What does the hostname command print?

It prints the name of the machine it runs on, once, on a single line, like my-laptop or web01.example.com; whether it's a short name or a fully qualified one depends on how the system is set up. I can't know your machine's name without running it.
Python: import socket; print(socket.gethostname()) - what's printed?
It prints the host name of the machine running the script, once, as a single line of text, like my-laptop. The name comes from that system's configuration, so I can't know it without running it.
Output of whoami?

`whoami` prints the username you're currently running as (the effective user), once, on a single line, like alice. With `sudo whoami` it prints root, because sudo runs commands as root by default. I can't know your username without running it.
echo "Hello, $(whoami)" - what will it say?
It prints one line: `Hello, ` followed by the username you're running as, like Hello, alice. It prints once per run, and I can't know your actual username without running it.
What does this print? import uuid; print(len(str(uuid.uuid4())))
It prints `36`, every time. The UUID itself is random, but its string form is always 32 hex digits plus 4 hyphens, which is 36 characters.
Python: import uuid; print(uuid.uuid4().version) - output?
It prints `4`, every time. uuid4() makes a new random UUID on each run, but its version field is always 4.
Tell me the output: import random; print(random.randint(7, 7))
It prints `7`, every time. random.randint includes both endpoints, so with both set to 7 the only possible result is 7.
What does console.log(Math.floor(Math.random())) print?
It prints `0`, every time. Math.random() always returns a value from 0 up to but not including 1, so Math.floor rounds it down to 0.
bash: what does echo $(( RANDOM % 1 )) print?
It prints `0`, every time. $RANDOM changes on each read, but any integer modulo 1 is 0.
On Linux, what does date -u -d @0 +%Y-%m-%d print?
It prints `1970-01-01`, every time. -d @0 sets the date to Unix time 0, the epoch, instead of the current time, and -u shows it in UTC, so the output doesn't depend on when you run it.
What day does this print? from datetime import date; print(date(2024, 2, 29).strftime('%A'))

It prints `Thursday`, every time. It formats the fixed date 29 February 2024, not today's date, and that day was a Thursday. The name is in English because Python keeps the C locale for dates unless the code changes it with locale.setlocale.
console.log(new Date(0).toISOString()) - output?

It prints `1970-01-01T00:00:00.000Z`, every time. new Date(0) is the Unix epoch, a fixed moment rather than the current time, and toISOString() always formats in UTC, so your time zone doesn't change it.
